# ISLA against the literature {#sec-isla-vs-geotransolver}

*Before this appendix:* @sec-landscape, for the families of neural PDE
surrogates and the terms used here, and @sec-isla, for ISLA's ideas.

**ISLA draws on the best parts of GLOBE and Transolver: from GLOBE the
boundary as the input, exact symmetry by construction, measure-weighted
sums and dimensionless geometry; from Transolver slice attention. What is
new in it is that combination and a short list of specific constructions
that make it work, each with a closest prior work that does part of it.** This
appendix states each idea against that prior work: what ISLA does, what the
prior work does, what is new, the evidence in this book, and the caveat. It
ends with the contributions that matter most, ideas from the literature
worth trying, a table of published numbers for orientation, and the
bibliography of the whole book. Ratios are baseline ÷ ISLA, above one
favoring ISLA, and the metric is the area-weighted relative L2 in float32
(@sec-metrics) under the reporting protocol (@sec-protocol).

```{python}
#| label: setup-literature
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import json
from pathlib import Path
import standing as S
LIM = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "campaigns_2026-10-23" / "book_E" / "limits_090.json"))
T2 = S.Standing("tensile2d")
T2_GT = [T2.fields[f].split(" (")[0] for f in T2.ds.headline if T2.verdict("GeoTransolver", f) == "trails"]
AZS = S.aerozoo()
AZA = {n.split()[0]: a for n, a in AZS["arms"].items()}
C_I, C_D = S.cost("aerozoo", "ISLA"), S.cost("aerozoo", "ISLA-DTT")
STL = LIM["remesh"]["drivaerml_volume"]["stl"]
TH = LIM["theta"]["pressure_ratio"]
```

## What each is {#sec-vs-what}

**GeoTransolver and ISLA share the slice mechanism and differ in what the
network may see.** Transolver (Wu et al., 2024; @sec-vs-bibliography)
routes every point softly into slices with a softmax over slices, forms
each slice state as a count-weighted mean of its points, attends among the
slices and reads the result back (@sec-landscape-cost). GeoTransolver
(Adams et al., 2025) adds a cross-attention in every block to a shared
embedding of the geometry and the global parameters, built once from
multi-scale ball queries. Both read raw point coordinates
and the problem's global vector as a feature, and both learn pose, scale
and the mesher's habits from data. Their reference configurations in this
book are GeoTransolver at width 256 and Transolver at width 512 with 16
layers; what each sees, and the protocol, are in @sec-baselines.

**ISLA** (width 512, 12 layers, 512 slices) combines the slice mechanism
with the principles of GLOBE (Sharpe, 2025), a boundary-integral surrogate
whose field is a sum of learned kernels from the boundary faces to the
target (@sec-landscape-globe): the boundary as the input, the rigid-motion
symmetry built into the architecture, sums over the boundary weighted by
the cells' measure, and dimensionless geometry (@sec-isla). No coordinate
reaches a learned map. Every sum over the boundary is a measure-weighted quadrature
rule. Position is stated only as invariants of a token against the slices'
own anchors, in a length unit computed from the boundary. Vector and tensor
outputs are rebuilt at the end from a basis that rotates with the body. The
slice sublayer reads the normalized state. The forward pass with every
tensor shape is @sec-architecture, and the contracts it holds to roundoff
are @sec-isla-contracts.

## The standing in one sentence {#sec-vs-standing}

**In distribution, ISLA leads on some datasets and fields and trails on
others. Rotated and translated, or resampled, its error barely moves except
on the lug's structured mesh, whose nodes tie for their closest feature,
where the class's tie rule removes most of the growth (@sec-limits-ties,
@sec-standing-geometry), while
the baselines' errors grow by factors.**

```{python}
#| label: para-vs-standing
#| output: asis
keys = S.final()        # a cross-dataset count reads the final standings; S.tally_note() names the ones it leaves out
flight = S.in_flight()
cells = []          # (dataset, field label, baseline, verdict)
for k in keys:
    s = S.Standing(k)
    for f in s.ds.headline:
        for b in S.BASELINES:
            if s.has(b):
                cells.append((s.ds.name, s.fields[f], b, s.verdict(b, f)))
held = [(S.DATASETS[k].short, S.Standing(k).fields[f]) for k in keys for f in S.DATASETS[k].provisional]
def az_verdict(b, f, split="full"):
    """The seed rule of standing.Standing.verdict on one AeroZoo split."""
    cb, ci = AZA[b]["splits"][split][f], AZA["ISLA"]["splits"][split][f]
    bs, i = list(cb["per_seed"].values()), list(ci["per_seed"].values())
    if abs(cb["mean"] / ci["mean"] - 1) < S.TIE_BAND:
        return "is level with"
    return "leads" if min(bs) > max(i) else "trails" if max(bs) < min(i) else "is level with"
cells += [("AeroZoo", AZS["fields"]["velocity_l2"], b, az_verdict(b, "velocity_l2")) for b in S.BASELINES if "full" in AZA[b]["splits"]]
az_p = {b: AZA[b]["splits"]["full"]["pressure_l2"]["mean"] / AZA["ISLA"]["splits"]["full"]["pressure_l2"]["mean"] for b in S.BASELINES if "full" in AZA[b]["splits"]}
cells = [c for c in cells if c[3] != "is not compared with"]
n = len(cells)
lead = [c for c in cells if c[3] == "leads"]
trail = [c for c in cells if c[3] == "trails"]
level = len([c for c in cells if c[3] == "is level with"])
assert len(lead) + len(trail) + level == n
def group(cs):
    by = {}
    for ds, fl, b, _ in cs:
        by.setdefault(ds, []).append(f"{fl} against {b}")
    return "; ".join(f"{ds} ({', '.join(v)})" for ds, v in by.items())
posed_isla, posed_base, bent = [], [], []
for k in keys:
    s = S.Standing(k)
    for f in s.ds.headline:
        r = s.shift("ISLA", f, "posed")
        (bent if abs(r - 1) > 0.02 else posed_isla).append((s.ds.name, s.fields[f], r))
        posed_base += [s.shift(b, f, "posed") for b in S.BASELINES if s.has(b)]
bent_ds = {}
for ds, fl, r in bent:
    if ds != S.DATASETS["lug"].name:   # the lug has its own clause below
        bent_ds[ds] = max(bent_ds.get(ds, 1.0), r)
print(f"At the reference configurations on the native mesh, over {len(keys)} datasets and AeroZoo's in-distribution split, {n} comparisons "
      f"(each headline field against each baseline, by the seed rule of @sec-fair-comparison), ISLA leads in {len(lead)}"
      + (f" ({nl} of them on the lug against Transolver, which reads no boundary-condition labels there)"
         if (nl := sum("lug" in c[0] and c[2] == "Transolver" for c in lead)) else "")
      + f", "
      f"is level in {level} and trails in {len(trail)}. It trails on: {group(trail)}. " + (S.tally_note() + " " if S.tally_note() else "")
      + "AeroZoo counts on velocity only: on its "
      "pressure both baselines are about a zero predictor, so " + " and ".join(f"{b} ÷ ISLA {S.fmt_ratio(r)}" for b, r in az_p.items())
      + " there compare ISLA with predicting zero (@sec-aerozoo-baselines). "
      + "".join(f"{d} {fl} is not counted: the baselines' error on it includes an out-of-plane component that ISLA's "
                "planar prediction does not have (@sec-interior-airfrans). " for d, fl in held) +
      f"Rotated and translated, ISLA's error moves by at most "
      f"{100 * max(abs(r - 1) for *_, r in posed_isla):.1f}% on every headline field of the final standings"
      + (" but the lug's" if "lug" in keys else "")
      + (" except on " + " and ".join(f"the {ds} (up to ×{r:.2f})" for ds, r in bent_ds.items()) if bent_ds else "")
      + "; on the GINOT bracket lug ISLA's error is "
      f"×{S.Standing('lug').shift('ISLA', 'von_mises_l2', 'posed'):.2f} rotated and translated, where its structured mesh ties interior "
      "nodes for their closest feature in the geometry the standings trained with, a growth the class's tie rule mostly removes "
      "(@sec-limits-ties); "
      f"the baselines' errors grow by factors of {min(posed_base):.1f} to {max(posed_base):.0f}.")
notes = [S.DATASETS[k] for k in keys if not S.DATASETS[k].reference]
if notes:
    print("\n\n" + " ".join(f"On {d.name}, ISLA's checkpoints are of the raw-read variant: its slice pooling "
                             f"and broadcast read the raw stream." for d in notes))
print("\n\nData: " + ", ".join(S.Standing(k).source for k in keys + flight) + ", results/char/aerozoo_090.json. The standing row by row is @sec-standing.")
print()
print(S.in_flight_callout("lug"))
```

## Ideas, one at a time {#sec-vs-novel}

**The ideas below run from new, in the sense a paper needs (no prior work
found does it, and the book measures what it does), through adoptions
applied in a new place, to engineering. Each says which it is.** Each is
stated as what ISLA does, the closest prior work, what is new, the
evidence, and the caveat. Every source is in @sec-vs-bibliography.

### Measure-weighted slice routing, and discretization consistency as the acceptance criterion {#sec-vs-novel-measure}

*What ISLA does.* The routing softmax over points adds the log cell
measure as a bias, so every slice state is a quadrature estimate of a
surface integral and inherits Horvitz–Thompson consistency under any
sampling law (@sec-isla-quadrature). A change to the architecture is
adopted only if the prediction converges to one field under refinement and
to the same field under two sampling laws (@sec-principled-decisions).

*Prior work.* Neural operators are defined by convergence under refinement
(Kovachki et al., 2023), and the graph kernel network evaluates its kernel
integral as a quadrature sum (Li et al., 2020). Cao (2021) reads attention
as a kernel integral; Berner et al. (2026) state the general recipe of
quadrature weights in the normalization and aggregation of attention, so
that a layer has one limit under refinement. Inducing points and latent
tokens decouple the discretization from the processor (Lee and Oh, 2024;
Wang and Wang, 2024). M³ treats the biased empirical measure of a mesh as
a training problem and rebalances the supervision (Mei et al., 2026). RIGNO
and GAOT report robustness to unseen resolutions (Mousavi et al., 2025;
Wen et al., 2025). GLOBE multiplies each face's kernel by the face's area,
so its boundary sums are quadratures (Sharpe, 2025). Transolver and
GeoTransolver weight each point once.

*What is new.* The form: a log-measure bias inside the point softmax of
slice routing, which turns a soft partition into a set of quadrature rules
and changes nothing else in the layer. The instruments: a biased inference
draw with exact inclusion weights and a training-law swap scored on an
independent draw (@sec-sampling-laws), which make "discretization
consistent" a measured readout rather than an asymptotic claim. And the
finding, which follows.

```{python}
#| label: para-vs-area
#| output: asis
rows = []
SURF = ("drivaerml_surface", "shift_suv")   # the compared surface standings with a uniform point cloud
for k in SURF:
    s = S.Standing(k)
    sh = {a: [s.shift(a, f, "area") for f in s.ds.headline] for a in S.ARCHS}
    rows.append((s.ds.name, sh))
lo = min(min(v) for _, sh in rows for a, v in sh.items() if a != "ISLA")
hi = max(max(v) for _, sh in rows for a, v in sh.items() if a != "ISLA")
isla = max(abs(x - 1) for _, sh in rows for x in sh["ISLA"])
print(f"**The finding.** On the two compared surface datasets whose uniform point cloud resamples the scored cells "
      f"({', '.join(n for n, _ in rows)}), the two released slice transformers' errors on the uniform point cloud "
      f"are {lo:.1f} to {hi:.1f} times their native-mesh errors on the headline fields, and ISLA's moves by at most "
      f"{100 * isla:.1f}%. Data: " + ", ".join(S.Standing(k).source for k in SURF) + ".")
```

No benchmark had exposed this dependence, because every benchmark scores
on the sampling it trains on.

*Evidence.* The point-cloud column of every surface standing
(@sec-standing); the sampling-law instruments of @sec-sampling-laws; the
measure-weights row of the design ledger (@sec-principled-ledger). The
property is portable: GeoTransolver and Transolver given ISLA's
measure-weighted pooling and a Horvitz–Thompson-centered datapipe, an
ablation that leaves the released baselines unmodified, are consistent under
the biased draw too (@sec-robustness-density).

*Caveat.* Measure-weighted boundary sums are adopted from GLOBE, and
quadrature-weighted attention from the neural-operator literature; the routing form, the instruments and the
factors are what is new. An interior prediction point takes its wall
distance and direction from the exact closest point of the full-resolution
surface, the same for every draw of the boundary tokens
(@sec-exact-geometry-draw), so ISLA needs the wall at the precision of the
mesh the interior was built on: a watertight STL in place of the CFD wall of
the DrivAerML car raises its interior error
`{python} " / ".join(f"{STL[f]:.2f}" for f in ("pressure_l2", "velocity_l2", "nut_l2"))`
times on pressure, velocity and eddy viscosity, all of it next to the wall
(@sec-limits-boundary-law).

### An origin-free frame with an integral length unit {#sec-vs-novel-frame}

*What ISLA does.* No center reaches a learned map; ISLA-DTT's cluster
forest uses a canonical frame of the boundary only to group cells for
speed (@sec-arch-tree-read). Positions enter only as differences from the slices'
own anchors, and the one length unit is the
measure-weighted RMS pairwise distance of the full-resolution boundary, a
two-point integral that is exact for the meshed boundary and converges under
refinement (@sec-isla-frame).

*Prior work.* Translation invariance through relative positions is the
standard construction of equivariant message passing. EGNN builds its
messages from relative squared distances and updates positions by weighted
sums of relative vectors (Satorras et al., 2021); MeshGraphNets encode
relative positions on mesh edges (Pfaff et al., 2021); message-passing PDE
solvers carry relative positions in their messages (Brandstetter et al.,
2022). All of them take differences between *neighbors* on a graph. GLOBE
states every position relative to a boundary face, in units of reference
lengths it is given (Sharpe, 2025). Frame
averaging (Puny et al., 2022) and learned canonicalization (Kaba et al.,
2023) instead fix a frame from the input, which is what a canonical frame
does for GeoTransolver in @sec-pose.

*What is new.* The reference points are neither neighbors nor a centroid
but the data-adaptive anchors of a global slice partition, so a transformer
with no neighborhoods and no positional encoding is exactly
translation-invariant. The length unit is chosen for its estimator
properties: measure-weighted, center-free, and invisible to a rescale of the
weights alone. Neither piece is deep; together they let a slice transformer
be given no coordinate at all.

*Evidence.* The contracts (@sec-isla-contracts); the pose column of every
standing (@sec-standing); the length-unit row of the design ledger
(@sec-principled-ledger).

*Caveat.* A component of the architecture, argued by its contracts; not a
result on its own.

### A scalar trunk on invariants, and an equivariant output basis {#sec-vs-novel-invariants}

*What ISLA does.* Every learned map sees only norms and dot products of
the vectors a token has: its separation from an anchor, its normal, the
anchor's normal, the global directions. Vectors and tensors are rebuilt
once, at the output, as invariant coefficients times directions that move
with the body (@sec-isla-relational, @sec-isla-heads).

*Prior work.* "Scalarize, compute on invariants, vectorize in a local
frame" is the ClofNet construction (Du et al., 2022), and in spirit
GemNet's distance, angle and dihedral invariants (Gasteiger et al., 2021).
PaiNN keeps a separate vector stream (Schütt et al., 2021). Vector Neurons
lift every neuron to a 3-vector (Deng et al., 2021). Tensor field networks,
SE(3)-Transformers, Equiformer and e3nn carry irreducible representations
through every layer (Thomas et al., 2018; Fuchs et al., 2020; Liao and
Smidt, 2023; Geiger and Smidt, 2022). GATr works in the projective geometric
algebra (Brehmer et al., 2023), and AB-GATr brings it to the anchored
architecture of AB-UPT (Rygiel et al., 2026). EqGINO makes a geometry-informed
Fourier operator exactly equivariant to the discrete symmetries of its grid
(Kim et al., 2026). GLOBE builds a translation-, rotation- and
parity-equivariant surrogate from Green's-function-like kernels evaluated
from boundary faces to targets, each on parity-even invariants of the
face–target pair with vector outputs rebuilt on the pair's true vectors
(Sharpe, 2025). Most of these pay for
equivariance inside every layer.

*What is new.* The choice to keep the entire trunk an ordinary scalar
transformer and pay for equivariance once, at the edges, in an
industrial-scale slice transformer, and the measurement of what that costs
against two non-equivariant baselines on every dataset of the standing (@sec-standing). The
contrast in the literature is the price of the per-layer route: Rygiel et
al. (2026) report AB-GATr at 2 to 11 times the training time of AB-UPT. A
second element is small and sharp. Scalar heads on invariants are
reflection-invariant, so a target that is one frame component of a tensor
(a stress $\sigma_{12}$, a displacement along one of the dataset's axes) is representable
only as a view of a predicted tensor (@sec-isla-heads). A third is a rule:
every input ISLA takes is a datum of the PDE problem, and a dataset's own
axes are excluded even where they would buy accuracy (@sec-pose-prior).

*Evidence.* The contracts; the pose columns of @sec-standing; the
tensor-valued targets of PLAID Tensile2d (@sec-tensile2d); the pose-prior
diagnostic (@sec-pose-prior).

*Caveat.* Covariance itself is not new; its placement and its measured
price are. The cost is reported as the in-distribution standing, which
holds leads and deficits by dataset (@sec-vs-standing), not as an
across-the-board parity.

### Soft anchors and point-to-anchor invariants as the positional encoding {#sec-vs-novel-anchors}

*What ISLA does.* Each slice forms, from its own routing weights, a mean
position and a mean normal. Every token's position is then a handful of
invariant scalars per anchor, which refine the routing and are pooled back
into the token (@sec-isla-slices, @sec-isla-relational).

*Prior work.* Soft assignment of many inputs to a few latent tokens is
Transolver's slice (Wu et al., 2024), the Perceiver's latent array (Jaegle
et al., 2021), the Set Transformer's inducing points (Lee et al., 2019),
UPT's latent tokens (Alkin et al., 2024) and Slot Attention's slots, whose
softmax runs over slots so that slots compete for inputs (Locatello et al.,
2020). In all of these the latent token is a weighted mean of *features*,
and input positions enter as features too. GeoTransolver cross-attends
every block to a shared geometry embedding (Adams et al., 2025). Hu et al.
(2026) argue that the value of physics attention lies in the slice and
deslice operations rather than in the attention among slices.

*What is new.* Anchors as geometric aggregates, a position and a normal,
that move with the body, and a token's relation to that constellation as
its only knowledge of where it is: a data-adaptive, equivariant,
coordinate-free positional encoding. No prior work found forms slice
positions and uses them this way. The trained partitions of
@sec-arch-routing-trained are its picture.

*Evidence.* The trained routing (@sec-arch-routing-trained); the
relational-invariant ablations of @sec-isla-relational.

*Caveat.* The anchors are formed from the geometry, so where the geometry
barely varies between cases they barely move, and positional resolution is
then only as fine as the partition. PLAID Tensile2d, one specimen family whose
outline stays a tension specimen, is the dataset where that bound would bind, and
GeoTransolver leads there on `{python} " and ".join(T2_GT)` (@sec-tensile2d).
Whether the bound is the cause is not measured.

### Normalized slice reads {#sec-vs-novel-norm}

*What ISLA does.* The slice sublayer's routing, its pooling into slice
states and its broadcast back to the tokens all read the normalized state
$\operatorname{LN}(h)$. The raw stream $h$ enters the block only through
the residual identity and the MLP's LayerNorm. Each block is then a pre-LN
block in the sense of @sec-landscape-block: its updates have a size set by
its weights, and the stream grows by addition (@sec-isla-layer).

*Prior work.* The pre-LN block normalizes the input of each sublayer and
leaves the residual stream unnormalized (Xiong et al., 2020). The sandwich
and peri-LN blocks also normalize each sublayer's output (Ding et al., 2021;
Kim et al., 2025). QK-normalization normalizes queries and keys and bounds
every attention score (Henry et al., 2020; Dehghani et al., 2023). The
normalized transformer keeps every state on the unit sphere (Loshchilov et
al., 2024). Transolver's blocks are pre-LN.

*What is new.* Little in the principle, which is the pre-LN discipline. The
contribution is its application to a sublayer with three reads of the
state, two of them hidden inside a geometry-weighted pooling and broadcast,
and the mechanism it removes: a sublayer that concatenates the raw state
into a linear map multiplies the stream by a fixed factor per block, and
twelve such blocks multiply it geometrically (@sec-isla-normalized-reads).

*Evidence.* The raw-read ablation on DeepJEB++, whose validation loss
rises and never recovers while the normalized reads train through
(@sec-deepjeb-ladders); the reference-configuration standings
(@sec-standing).

*Caveat.* The normalized read is adopted, not invented. Its accuracy effect is measured
against the raw-read variant, an ablation, and not against other
normalization placements. It stops at the slice sublayer: the frame of
the equivariant head reads the raw stream, and on DeepJEB++ its anchors
concentrate on about one point (@sec-deepjeb-ladders). A normalized input
for the head frame, a candidate fix for its logit growth, was tested and
not adopted.

### Cosine routing {#sec-vs-novel-cosine}

*What ISLA does.* The routing logit is a fixed temperature times the
cosine between the normalized token state and a prototype per slice,
synthesized per sample from learned base prototypes. Every content logit
is therefore bounded, so the content score cannot sharpen the routing
without limit as the weights grow (@sec-isla-slices).

*Prior work.* Scaled cosine attention in Swin Transformer V2 replaces the
dot product to stabilize training at scale (Liu et al., 2022);
QK-normalization bounds scores the same way (Henry et al., 2020).
Transolver++ addresses the opposite failure of slice weights, their
becoming uniform so that attention degenerates to average pooling, with a
per-point adaptive temperature and a Gumbel-softmax (Luo et al., 2025).
Load-balancing losses in sparse expert routing target the same family of
failure (Fedus et al., 2022).

*What is new.* Nothing in the mechanism; ISLA applies bounded logits to
slice routing.

*Evidence.* The routing design row (@sec-principled-ledger) and the
trained routing (@sec-arch-routing-trained).

*Caveat.* The bound is on the content score; the geometric refinement
added to it is not bounded, and the bound does not by itself prevent
routing that is too soft or too concentrated for the task.

### Read-only prediction points with a tree-evaluated boundary read {#sec-vs-novel-tree}

*What ISLA does.* ISLA-DTT (`query_independent=True`) makes interior
prediction points passive readers: they carry no routing mass, so they
never write into the slices, and after every block each one also reads
the whole boundary through a learned kernel of relative geometry and an
attention over cell states, weighted by cell measure and evaluated with a
Barnes–Hut forest. A
prediction is then a function of its point and the boundary alone, and it
does not change with the other points requested (@sec-arch-modes).

*Prior work.* DeepONet's trunk evaluates each query point independently
(Lu et al., 2021). Perceiver IO, UPT and AB-UPT decode query points by
cross-attention to a latent or anchor set (Jaegle et al., 2022; Alkin et
al., 2024; Alkin et al., 2025). Boundary-integral learners represent the
solution as a learned kernel from the boundary to the target: DeepGreen
and BI-GreenNet learn Green's functions (Gin et al., 2021; Lin et al.,
2022), BENO embeds boundary geometry and data in a Green's-function-motivated
operator (Wang et al., 2024), and GLOBE evaluates such kernels from
boundary faces to targets, each target independently of the others
(Sharpe, 2025); its PhysicsNeMo code does so with the cluster tree that
ISLA-DTT's forest is built from, an approximation that vanishes as the
opening angle $\theta \to 0$. The Barnes–Hut tree evaluates an
$N$-body sum in $O(N \log N)$ (Barnes and Hut, 1986), and Erwin builds a
hierarchical transformer on a ball tree (Zhdanov et al., 2025).

*What is new.* The combination: a learned, measure-weighted boundary
integral at every depth of a slice transformer, evaluated with a
Barnes–Hut forest so that every prediction point reads every boundary
cell, beside read-only access to the slices.

*Evidence.* Under every change of the request probed on AirfRANS its
error moves by at most
`{python} f"{LIM['query_population']['dtt_max_abs_dev']:.0e}"`, float32
roundoff, where the interacting form's moves by factors
(@sec-limits-query-independence). Refining the airfoil moves the pressure
error of the ISLA-DTT pair trained with the compiled path before its fault
was fixed by up to `{python} f"{100 * (max(TH['1.0']) - 1):.0f}"`% at its
trained opening angle $\theta = 1$ and by
`{python} f"{100 * (max(TH['0']) - 1):.1f}"`% at $\theta = 0$, the size of
the tree's approximation (@sec-oq-dtt-frame). The interior chapters measure
it against the interacting form (@sec-drivaerml, @sec-airfrans), and the
AeroZoo held-out splits decide which of the two is ISLA's interior form
(@sec-oq-dtt).

*Caveat.* Which interior form is the better default is an open question
(@sec-oq-dtt). The read costs time and memory: on AeroZoo `full` its median
training step is `{python} f"{C_D['step_seconds'] / C_I['step_seconds']:.1f}"`
times the interacting form's and its peak memory
`{python} f"{C_D['peak_gib'] / C_I['peak_gib']:.2f}"` times (@tbl-ref-cost). Where the canonical frame the forest is built in ties, a rotation
regroups clusters and moves the read only by the tree's error.

### The general boundary interface {#sec-vs-novel-interface}

*What ISLA does.* One class reads $K$ global unit directions, $S$ global
scalars, the boundary as named conditions, each with its own per-cell fields
of declared rank (scalar, vector, second-order tensor) and its own input
layer, and interior prediction points, and predicts fields of
any of those ranks. The same class trains on cars, wings, airfoils, a
tensile specimen, a lug and a family of brackets (@sec-isla-inputs,
@sec-isla-conditions, @sec-arch-modes). GLOBE keys its boundary conditions
by name the same way, with a kernel per condition in every layer; ISLA
gives each condition its own input layer and shares its slice layers.

*Prior work.* GNOT's heterogeneous normalized attention takes several
input functions, geometries and parameters (Hao et al., 2023). BENO embeds
boundary geometry and inhomogeneous boundary values (Wang et al., 2024).
GINOT feeds loading conditions beside the surface point cloud and decodes
queries by attention (Liu et al., 2025). Message-passing PDE solvers put
boundary conditions and PDE parameters in their messages (Brandstetter et
al., 2022). Mousavi et al. (2026) extend boundary data into the domain as a
learned field so that any domain-to-domain operator can consume it.

*What is new.* The typed contract: directions enter as unit vectors and
magnitudes as scalars for every model, a component target is a view of a
tensor output, every input is a datum of the PDE problem, and every channel
keeps the covariance contracts under test.

*Evidence.* The contract tests (@sec-isla-contracts); the structural
datasets, whose loads and conditions enter through this interface alone
(@sec-tensile2d, @sec-lug, @sec-deepjeb).

*Caveat.* Interface design, not a mechanism.

### The fused geometry kernel {#sec-vs-novel-kernel}

*What ISLA does.* The per-layer geometry region (anchors, relational
invariants, routing refinement, pooling) runs in one Triton kernel per
direction that never stores the $N \times M \times (\text{invariants})$
array and recomputes it in the backward pass (@sec-architecture).

*Prior work.* Transolver-3 tiles the slice computation and reorders its
matrix products to reach meshes of over 160 million cells (Zhou et al.,
2026). Transolver++ ships a parallel implementation for million-point
inputs (Luo et al., 2025). Memory-efficient attention kernels never store
the score array (Dao et al., 2022). Activation recomputation is standard.

*What is new.* Nothing conceptually; it is what lets ISLA's per-slice
geometry run at 200,000 cells per case (@sec-architecture).

*Caveat.* Engineering.

## Which contributions matter most {#sec-vs-ranked}

**Ranked by how much is new and how much evidence stands behind it.**

1. **Discretization consistency as a measured property, and the dependence
   of the released slice transformers on the sampling law**
   (@sec-vs-novel-measure). The instruments, the factors on two surface
   datasets, and the one-term mechanism that removes the dependence.
   Self-contained and reproducible.
2. **Exact rigid-motion covariance in a slice transformer, paid for at the
   edges** (@sec-vs-novel-frame, @sec-vs-novel-invariants,
   @sec-vs-novel-anchors together): the anchor-relative invariant
   construction, its contracts, and its cost measured as the
   in-distribution standing on every dataset, with the component clause of
   the scalar heads as a corollary.
3. **Read-only prediction points with a tree-evaluated boundary read**
   (@sec-vs-novel-tree): a query-independent interior form whose evidence
   sits in the interior chapters.
4. **Normalized slice reads and cosine routing** (@sec-vs-novel-norm,
   @sec-vs-novel-cosine): adoptions, worth a section on why a slice
   sublayer must read the normalized state.
5. **The general interface and the fused kernel** (@sec-vs-novel-interface,
   @sec-vs-novel-kernel): engineering.

## Ideas from the literature worth trying {#sec-vs-ideas}

**The comparison turns up experiments worth doing, each aimed at a named
weakness.** None of them is run in this book; the open questions they bear
on are in @sec-open-questions.

- a per-token adaptive routing temperature, after Transolver++ (Luo et
  al., 2025), as a control on the fixed temperature of cosine routing;
- a measure-weighted local aggregation among interior prediction points,
  after GeoTransolver's ball queries, DoMINO and GAOT (Ranade et al., 2025;
  Wen et al., 2025), for the interior pressure deficit against both baselines on the AirfRANS interior task (@sec-limits-interior);
- reflection-odd invariants (a triple product of a token's normal, a
  global direction and its separation from an anchor) for frame-component
  targets, after GATr, whose multivector features are typed by grade
  (Brehmer et al., 2023); GLOBE, like ISLA's trunk, stays
  parity-equivariant through parity-even invariants and true vectors
  alone (Sharpe, 2025);
- a measure-weighted training loss, after M³ (Mei et al., 2026), for any
  remaining dependence on the training sampling law;
- inter-slice attention as a control, after Hu et al. (2026);
- an externally run benchmark, CarBench on DrivAerNet++ (Elrefaie et al.,
  2025), for a held-out confirmation outside this book's experiments;
- the published GINOT numbers on the bracket lug (Liu et al., 2025),
  re-scored on this book's split, to say whether ISLA's lead there is a lead
  over the field or only over the two baselines.

Two families are already in the class. Query-independent decoding, the
AB-UPT, UPT and Perceiver IO route, is ISLA-DTT (@sec-vs-novel-tree).
Canonicalization, the frame-averaging route, is measured on GeoTransolver
in @sec-pose and is what the pose contract is compared against.

## Published numbers for orientation {#sec-vs-published}

**Published numbers on DrivAerML exist, and none of them is comparable with
this book's or with each other's.** @tbl-vs-published gives them as the
papers report them so a reader can place the magnitudes. Each paper uses
its own split, its own number of points, its own error norm and its own
normalization. This book's metric divides by the norm of the standardized
label (@sec-metrics), which none of them does.

| source | model | error measure | surface pressure | wall shear | volume pressure | volume velocity |
|:---|:---|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Alkin et al. (2025), Table 4 | AB-UPT | relative L2 [%], protocol A | 3.82 | – | – | 5.93 |
| Alkin et al. (2025), Table 4 | Transolver | relative L2 [%], protocol A | 4.81 | – | – | 6.78 |
| Alkin et al. (2025), Table 4 | UPT | relative L2 [%], protocol A | 7.44 | – | – | 8.74 |
| Alkin et al. (2025), Table 4 | GINO | relative L2 [%], protocol A | 13.03 | – | – | 40.58 |
| Adams et al. (2025), Table 2 | GeoTransolver, 20 layers, 29M parameters | relative L1 [%], protocol B | 2.86 | 4.9 | 3.09 | 4.02 |

: Published DrivAerML errors, copied from the cited tables, for orientation
only. Protocol A: a random split of 400 training, 34 validation and 50 test
cases, scored over the full point cloud in passes of 16,000 surface and
16,000 volume points. Protocol B: 48 test designs. How to read this: the
two sources use different norms (relative L2 against relative L1), splits
and point counts, and neither uses this book's standardized-label
denominator, so no number here may be compared with the other source's
rows or with any number in this book; the book's own comparisons are in
@sec-standing. {#tbl-vs-published}
